rv.q: Those with strong memories of the superb 1992 revival starring Nathan Lane, Faith Prince and Peter Gallagher will find much to quibble about here.
There's an overriding flatness to what should be a sensational high-roller affair, sparking to life occasionally only to sag again under the strain.

Oddly cast and oppressively overproduced, the show is so busy with dizzying cinematic scenery, hard-edge choreography and updated musical arrangements that it's hard to find the people, much less the pulse.
Whatever special substance it is that makes old shows feel new-born and artificial musicals ring truer than life, this “Guys and Dolls” left it behind in the laboratory.

"Guys and Dolls" is one of the great shows in American musical-theater history. Its colorful characters, based on the creations of Damon Runyon; rapturously wonderful songs by Frank Loesser and distinctive comic sensibility fit together with rare perfection.
Though the show is always in motion, due in large part to a giant LED screen, it still feels static.
But there is something essentially disappointing about this production.
And if anyone is to blame, it is director Des McAnuff (“Jersey Boys”), whose new Broadway revival is a misconceived fiasco.
Overall though, this "Guys and Dolls" delivers a cascade of delights, including the arrival of that Broadway belter, Mary Testa, as Gen. Matilida B. Cartwright of the Salvation Army.
This is a show where a lot of joy washes over the audience in spite of the fact that the songs are over-miked and the talk scenes between the numbers don't sparkle as much.

tn.cat: Best Scenic Design of a Musical

cn.t: A misconceived revival that buries a nearly perfect musical under overproduction and pallid performances. The brilliant Loesser score provides some pleasure, but critics find it flatfooted and uninspired compared to superior past productions.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Nederlander Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here. Note: Nederlander Theatre itself warns of limited legroom in some orchestra rows.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out. As with the rest of the orchestra here, legroom can be tight in some rows.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well. As with the rest of the orchestra here, legroom can be tight in some rows.
A noticeable side angle, but Nederlander Theatre's more moderate size keeps the distance from the stage manageable.

vs.sum: An older theater in need of renovation, with virtually no rake in the orchestra — a tall person seated in front will block your view. First mezzanine row has a horizontal safety bar that partially obstructs sightlines. Legroom is tight throughout.

acc.note: Step-free main entrance to Orchestra. 6 wheelchair spaces. Personal induction loop devices available.
